messages.text: Walk me through how EcoSmartLoop and Oakminder keep people in the loop, in detail.

claims.text: EcoSmartLoop pauses at three bins so a person confirms each sort before the agent acts on it, which keeps a human decision at the one step where a wrong sort costs the most.
The pause shows the item, the bin the agent would choose and why, so the person can accept the sort in one press or move the item to another bin before anything happens.
Each correction a person makes at the pause is kept with the item, so the next time a similar item arrives the agent proposes the bin that the person chose rather than its first guess.
When the agent is unsure it says so at the pause instead of choosing quietly, and the item waits for a person rather than going to the most likely bin by default.
For Oakminder, Steve chose Convex to make real-time data changes easier to build, pairing it with Expo, Clerk, and RevenueCat, so a change one person makes shows up for everyone at once.
Oakminder suggests a reminder but leaves the person to confirm it, so nothing is scheduled on their behalf without a press that says yes, and a dismissed suggestion stays dismissed.
Because the data updates live, two people sharing a list see each other's confirmations as they happen, which keeps both of them in the loop without a refresh or a separate message.

Across both projects the pattern is the same: the software proposes, a person decides at a clearly marked step, and the decision is remembered so the next proposal is closer to what that person wants.
Neither project hides the step where a person is needed behind a setting; the pause in EcoSmartLoop and the confirm in Oakminder are part of the main flow every time.
The case studies describe these steps as deliberate design choices rather than limits, chosen so that the people using each product can trust what the software does on their behalf.
